A_admissions_architecture.primary_application_route: The Central Applications Office (CAO) is the near-universal centralized platform for EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants applying to full-time undergraduate courses at Irish Higher Education Institutions (universities, Technological Universities, and other HEIs). CAO is a private company (Central Applications Office Ltd., registered in Ireland, based in Galway) jointly owned and operated by the participating HEIs, not a government body. Critically, CAO is NOT merely a registration/routing layer like Studielink or UCAS: for the large majority of 'points' (non-restricted) courses, CAO's own system computes a ranked list of all eligible applicants by their Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) points score and automatically issues offers to the highest-ranked applicants up to the number of places the HEI has specified for that course code, with no separate per-application human review at the university for most courses. Admission decisions remain formally and legally the HEIs' — each HEI sets the entry requirements, subject prerequisites, and place count per course code and instructs CAO how to process it (Citizens Information, a statutory information body: 'The HEIs decide who gets places on their courses and they tell the CAO to make offers to successful candidates... all decisions on admissions are made by the individual institutions and not by the CAO') — but the moment-to-moment ranking/allocation execution is a shared, centrally-run computation, not an act of individual human review per application for standard courses.
A_admissions_architecture.centralized_or_decentralized: Hybrid, but a structurally different hybrid from the UK, Netherlands, or Italy. Application processing AND the points-ranking/allocation execution are centralized in CAO's shared system for the large majority of courses; setting entry requirements, subject prerequisites, and per-course place counts remains decentralized to each HEI, which then instructs CAO how to process its own course codes. Restricted-application courses (Medicine, Art & Design, Architecture, etc.) layer an HEI-run early assessment (portfolio, interview, aptitude test) on top of this shared points mechanism rather than replacing it. Non-EU/international applicants generally sit outside this architecture entirely, applying direct to each HEI's own international admissions office.
major_application_platforms: CAO (Central Applications Office) — the required route for essentially all EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status full-time undergraduate applicants; some non-EU applicants may also be instructed by a specific HEI to apply through CAO (e.g., for visa-timing reasons), but this is HEI-specific, not the default for non-EU applicants

Each HEI's own direct international-admissions portal (e.g., UCD's www.ucd.ie/apply, Trinity's course-specific 'Non-EU Application' pages) — the default route for non-EU/international-fee-status applicants
A_admissions_architecture.direct_university_application_possible: Yes, and it is the DEFAULT (not the exception) for non-EU/international-fee-status applicants: UCD's own registry states non-EU applicants 'apply direct to UCD, rather than through the Central Applications Office (CAO) like EU applicants,' and Trinity's non-EU applicants apply via a course-specific 'Non-EU Application' link with a separate per-course application fee. For EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants, direct application in place of CAO is generally NOT available for CAO-listed courses — UCD states explicitly that EU-fee-status applicants 'will only be admitted through the Central Applications Office (CAO) system,' in line with CAO and National University of Ireland (NUI) matriculation regulations. Fee status, not nationality alone, is the operative test (e.g., UK-citizen applicants who meet an Irish/EU residency requirement are still assessed for EU fees and must apply via CAO).
A_admissions_architecture.application_limit_if_any: Via CAO: up to 10 Level 8 (Honours Bachelor) course preferences and up to 10 Level 7/6 (Ordinary Bachelor / Higher Certificate) preferences — two separate ranked lists — per Citizens Information's official walkthrough of the CAO application form ('You can choose Level 8, Level 7, and Level 6 courses. You can add up to 10 courses at any (or all) of these levels'). No numerus-fixus-style cap on how many 'selective' or restricted courses may be chosen was found — unlike the Netherlands' 2-numerus-fixus cap, Ireland does not appear to need an equivalent rule, because virtually all Level 8 courses (not just a capped subset) already run through the same unified points-ranking mechanism. Direct non-EU applications to a given HEI are typically made and paid for per-course (e.g., Trinity: a separate EUR 55 fee per course application).
A_admissions_architecture.parallel_application_rules: A single CAO account holds one ranked list per level (Level 8; Level 7/6), covering all HEI/course combinations the applicant is interested in; CAO processes each course code according to that HEI's own instructed criteria, and the applicant receives a single unified stream of offers (by round) reflecting the highest-ranked eligible preference at each stage — structurally different from the non-EU/direct route, where an applicant submits and pays for a fully separate application per HEI (and sometimes per course) with no shared ranked-preference mechanism at all.
A_admissions_architecture.scope: platform (CAO mechanics) / national (EU-fee-status applicants' effective requirement to use CAO derives from joint HEI/NUI matriculation regulation, not a single statute naming CAO itself)

B_qualification_eligibility.recognition_mechanism: Two layers, structurally parallel to the Netherlands' Nuffic/university split. (1) QQI (Quality and Qualifications Ireland) hosts NARIC Ireland (the National Academic Recognition Information Centre, part of the ENIC-NARIC network) and publishes comparability statements comparing a foreign qualification to an Irish National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) award-type and level. QQI is explicit that this is advisory only: 'a comparability statement only provides advice and is not a legal document... decisions on recognising your qualification for employment, training or educational purposes will be made by the individual employer, competent authority or education and training admissions staff.' (2) For the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route specifically, the participating HEIs jointly author and agree a separate, more operational document — 'Agreed Entry Requirements for EU/EFTA/UK Applicants' — which sets country-by-country matriculation requirements and Indicative Points Score (IPS) conversion tables; the document itself states 'This document is produced jointly by the participating institutions and not CAO,' reinforcing that CAO executes but does not author admissions policy. For non-EU/EFTA/UK applicants (including Turkish nationals), neither of these documents applies directly — each HEI sets and publishes its own recognition/entry criteria independently (see Türkiye section).
B_qualification_eligibility.baseline_qualification_expectation: For the Leaving Certificate itself (and, via the joint EU/EFTA/UK document, for other European qualifications), the operative baseline is 'matriculation' — a floor separate from and prior to competitive points ranking. The CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines state the general Level 8 matriculation requirement is either (a) 6 subjects at Ordinary-level grade O6 or better, including 2 at Higher-level grade H5 or better, or (b) the same 6-subject O6 floor including 3 at H5 or better. Level 7/6 matriculation is normally 5 subjects at O5 or better. English must normally be included among the recognised subjects in all cases. The document is explicit that meeting this floor does NOT secure a place: 'entry to undergraduate courses in Ireland, and especially Level 8, is competitive and attainment of the minimum eligibility criteria does not guarantee a place. A points scoring system is in operation.'
B_qualification_eligibility.subject_prerequisites_general: Programme-specific, not decorative, but layered onto an à-la-carte Leaving Certificate rather than a Dutch-style fixed subject-combination ('profiel') structure — Irish students choose roughly 7-8 subjects individually from a wide list, without being forced into one of a small number of named national tracks. Many programmes (particularly STEM, Business, Economics, and health-science fields) require or strongly reward Higher Level Mathematics; a small number (e.g., Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, Engineering) specify additional science/maths subjects. See dedicated subject_prerequisites section.
B_qualification_eligibility.equivalency_process: For the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route: the jointly-agreed Guidelines document supplies country-specific matriculation tables and IPS conversion for roughly 30 European countries plus the International Baccalaureate, European Baccalaureate, and Ukrainian qualifications; qualifications outside this list (Appendix II: 'Non-EU qualifications,' e.g., African and Australian examination systems) are given only as indicative, non-binding guidance, with final assessment reserved to 'the relevant Higher Education Institution following receipt and verification of the applicant's official documentation.' For the non-EU/direct route: each HEI runs its own equivalency process; UCD and UCC both publish detailed per-programme, per-country tables (see Türkiye section) while Trinity instead names a short list of internationally portable qualifications (A-Level, IB, US High School Diploma + SAT/ACT) accepted for direct entry, routing everything else to its Foundation Programme.
B_qualification_eligibility.university_discretion: Substantial, and structurally central to this system in a way distinct from the Netherlands. Within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route, HEIs retain the power to set subject requirements and, crucially, the annual place count per course code that determines that year's emergent points cutoff — the same Leaving Certificate points total can be sufficient for one HEI's course and insufficient for another's, purely as a function of that course's specific applicant demand and place count. Within the non-EU/direct route, discretion is even more visible and openly documented: UCD, UCC, and Trinity apply materially different policies to the identical input qualification (a Turkish Lise Diplomasi) — see Türkiye section for the specific, sourced contrast.

credentials_covered.turkiye_meb: Turkish 'Lise Diploması' / 'Devlet Lise Diploması' (state general secondary school diploma) is NOT processed through the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK points system at all, since Turkey falls outside that document's scope; each HEI sets its own direct-entry policy — see dedicated Türkiye section below, which documents a genuine, sourced split between HEIs that accept it directly at a sufficient percentage (UCD, UCC) and one that does not accept it for direct entry at all (Trinity).
credentials_covered.ib_diploma: Processed through the CAO points system when an EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicant presents it: the Guidelines document gives an explicit IB-score-to-Indicative-Points-Score conversion table (e.g., 45 points = 600 IPS; 24 points = 350 IPS), plus a 25-point Higher Level Mathematics bonus (grade 4+) mirroring the Leaving Certificate bonus. Critically, CAO uses ACTUAL final IB results only, obtained directly from the IB organisation once the applicant's IB coordinator grants CAO access — not predicted grades (see Predicted grades section). For non-EU/direct applicants, IB is one of the qualifications Trinity names as accepted for direct undergraduate entry without a Foundation Programme.
credentials_covered.a_levels: Same treatment pattern as IB within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route (own country/qualification-specific matriculation and IPS table; GCSE English grade 4/C or better generally satisfies the English-language requirement). For non-EU/direct applicants, A-Levels are named by Trinity (and implicitly by UCD, which routes A-Level/IB applicants to separate curriculum-specific pages rather than the Lise-percentage table) as an accepted direct-entry qualification.
credentials_covered.ap_plus_us_diploma: Not addressed in the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' main country tables (the US is outside EU/EFTA/UK scope), but explicitly named by Trinity as an accepted direct non-EU entry route ('US High School Diploma with SAT or ACT'), and appears as an alternative route within UCD's Turkey-specific table for Turkish applicants who supplement a lower Lise Diplomasi percentage with a qualifying SAT score.
credentials_covered.french_bac: Covered within the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' country-by-country tables (France has its own dedicated section with matriculation and IPS conversion) for EU-fee-status applicants; not independently verified for the non-EU/direct route in this research pass.
credentials_covered.german_abitur: Covered within the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' country-by-country tables (Germany has its own dedicated section) for EU-fee-status applicants; not independently verified for the non-EU/direct route in this research pass.

turkiye_applicant_view.standard_diploma_sufficient_for_direct_e: Genuinely, sharply university-specific — the most non-uniform pattern found across the countries researched so far. Turkish nationals fall entirely outside the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK points system (Turkey is absent from that jointly-agreed document's ~30-country scope), so each HEI independently decides whether a plain Lise Diplomasi suffices. UCD (official Turkey-specific admissions table, 2026 entry) publishes direct per-programme percentage thresholds ranging from 67% Lise (e.g., BA Arts, History, English Literature) up to 100% Lise (e.g., Commerce, BSc Business, Computer Science, Engineering Omnibus, Architecture) — OR alternative routes combining a lower Lise percentage with either a partial Turkish university degree GPA (e.g., '71% Lise & 3.0/4.0 in degree') or a qualifying SAT score (e.g., '83% Lise & 1220 SAT'). UCC similarly publishes a tiered direct-entry system (67% / 85% / 90% Lise depending on programme competitiveness band) but additionally requires a passing result in Turkey's national university entrance exam (UCC's own page names it 'Lisans Yerleştirme Sınavı (LYS)' — the pre-2018 exam name, now superseded by YKS; this may indicate the page has not been updated to current Turkish exam terminology, a genuine data-quality caution rather than a confirmed current requirement). Trinity College Dublin, by contrast, does NOT accept the plain Lise Diplomasi for direct undergraduate entry at all: its official Turkey page states accepted qualifications for direct application are 'GCE A Levels, International Baccalaureate, US High School Diploma with SAT or ACT' only, and directs applicants without one of these to its International Foundation Programme. A Turkish applicant's eligibility for direct entry therefore cannot be assumed from one Irish university to the next.
turkiye_applicant_view.additional_qualifications_commonly_requi: Two patterns confirmed: (1) at HEIs like Trinity that do not accept the plain Lise Diplomasi at all, a full IB Diploma, A-Levels, or a US High School Diploma with a qualifying SAT/ACT score is required for direct entry; (2) at HEIs like UCD that do accept the plain Lise Diplomasi, applicants below the top percentage band can alternatively qualify via a qualifying SAT score layered on top of a lower Lise percentage, or via partial completion (GPA-based) of a Turkish university degree. UCC additionally documents accepted alternates including an 'Ön-Lisans Diplomasi' (associate degree) for its highest-competitiveness programme band.
turkiye_applicant_view.ap_ib_a_level_impact: Materially simplifies the picture, consistent with the pattern in every other country in this research package. At Trinity, IB/A-Level/AP-supported qualifications are the PRIMARY accepted direct-entry route for Turkish applicants (the plain Lise Diplomasi is not independently sufficient there at all). At UCD, IB and A-Level applicants are directed to separate, curriculum-specific entry-requirement pages rather than the Lise-percentage table, implying more standardised treatment than the country-specific negotiation a plain-diploma applicant faces.
turkiye_applicant_view.national_entrance_exam_relevance: Genuinely unresolved and inconsistent across the three universities sourced. UCC's published table names Turkey's national university entrance exam (under the outdated 'LYS' label) as a requirement layered on top of the Lise Diplomasi percentage for direct entry. UCD's detailed, programme-by-programme Turkey table makes no mention of YKS/LYS at all — its direct-entry routes are Lise-percentage-only, Lise+degree-GPA, or Lise+SAT. This should be recorded as a genuine, live cross-university difference — not resolved into one system-wide answer — and treated with additional caution given UCC's apparent use of superseded exam terminology (LYS was replaced by YKS in the 2018 Turkish exam reform).
turkiye_applicant_view.foundation_year_common: Yes, and it is the explicit, named fallback route at multiple HEIs for Turkish (and other non-EU) applicants who do not meet a given university's direct-entry bar. Trinity's International Foundation Programme is the stated route for any Turkish applicant without A-Level/IB/US-diploma-with-SAT/ACT. UCD separately operates an International Foundation Year 'for many programmes' for applicants who do not meet direct-entry requirements. Beyond the flagship universities, TU Dublin, Dublin City University, University College Cork, University of Limerick, Technological University of the Shannon, and private-partner colleges (e.g., Dublin International Foundation College, OnCampus Ireland) all publish International Foundation Programmes aimed at this population, typically one year long, with IELTS entry thresholds commonly cited around 4.5-5.5, some with guaranteed progression to a named degree programme on successful completion (e.g., TU Dublin).
turkiye_applicant_view.recognition_centralized_or_university_sp: University-specific, more decisively than in any other country covered by this research package so far. There is no CAO-run or QQI-run centralized Turkey-specific points conversion at all for non-EU-status Turkish applicants (QQI/NARIC Ireland's comparability statements are general and advisory, not admissions decisions, and CAO's jointly-agreed Guidelines document explicitly excludes non-EU/EFTA/UK qualifications from its scope). Each HEI independently authors, publishes, and can revise its own Turkey-specific (or Turkey-silent, in Trinity's case) policy. A Turkish applicant's acceptance at one Irish university carries no implication for any other.

academic_evidence_used.transcript_role: Within the CAO/points route, no separate transcript submission or holistic review occurs for standard courses — the points score is computed directly and mechanically from the applicant's official Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) results record, which CAO itself retrieves/receives from the State Examinations Commission (or, for IB, directly from the IB organisation once access is granted). Within the non-EU/direct route, a full transcript is a required, individually-reviewed document (alongside references, SOP, and English proficiency evidence).
academic_evidence_used.native_grades_handling: Within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route, each qualification type is read on its own scale via a jointly-agreed, qualification-specific conversion to a common 'Indicative Points Score' (IPS) — the Leaving Certificate's own H1-H8/O1-O8 scale IS the points scale (no conversion needed), while IB, A-Level, and ~30 other European qualifications each have their own explicit IPS conversion table in the Guidelines document; qualifications are never blended (the document states 'Two different examination types cannot be combined for scoring purposes'). Within the non-EU/direct route, native grades (e.g., a Turkish Lise Diploması percentage) are read directly against university-published percentage thresholds rather than converted to a universal GPA.
academic_evidence_used.predicted_grades_role: None, within the CAO/points route — see dedicated predicted_grades section; this holds even for IB/A-Level applicants whose home curricula natively produce predicted grades. Predicted grades DO appear to play a role within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route (see predicted_grades section).
academic_evidence_used.final_grades_role: Central and load-bearing for the CAO/points route: no offer for a standard course issues before actual final results are known, and the entire Round system is sequenced around the Leaving Certificate results-release date (21 August for the 2026 cycle). For the non-EU/direct route, final results are ultimately required to confirm/finalise a place, but an offer built on predicted or in-progress results can be made earlier (see predicted_grades and conditional_vs_unconditional sections).
academic_evidence_used.external_exams_role: The Leaving Certificate, for CAO points purposes, is entirely externally/nationally set and marked by the State Examinations Commission — unlike the Dutch VWO diploma's mixed school-set (schoolexamen) plus national (centraal examen) composite, there is no school-set continuous-assessment component feeding into the CAO points score for the mainstream Leaving Certificate. (The separate Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) track is a distinct, non-points-scored qualification and should not be conflated with the mainstream, CAO-points-scored Leaving Certificate.)
academic_evidence_used.course_rigor_signal: Read through explicit subject-level/grade-level prerequisites published per course (commonly a named minimum Higher Level Mathematics grade, sometimes a lab science) rather than a general 'rigor' holistic judgment; see subject_prerequisites section.
academic_evidence_used.standardized_tests: HPAT-Ireland (Medicine, all 6 medical schools) is the one nationally mandatory aptitude test within the domestic system; no SAT/ACT role within the CAO/points route. See dedicated standardized_tests section.

predicted_grades.are_used: Not within the CAO/points route, for any applicant category, in any curriculum. Ireland's system is explicitly described in official and semi-official sources as 'post-qualification admissions' — offers for standard courses are computed and issued only after actual final results are known. This is confirmed at its strongest for IB applicants specifically: the CAO Guidelines instruct May-sitting IB candidates to grant CAO direct electronic access to their ACTUAL final IB results once released, and CAO uses only that real result for points calculation — the IB's own native predicted-grade artifact (used operationally by UK/UCAS and, per this research package's Netherlands findings, by Dutch universities) plays no role in the CAO points process at all.
predicted_grades.where: Predicted grades DO appear to be used within the separate, HEI-run non-EU/direct-to-university application route: Trinity's general international undergraduate admissions page lists acceptable supporting documentation as 'Final high school exam results, OR Predicted Scores provided by your school' — explicitly naming predicted scores as sufficient at the application stage for non-EU applicants (who commonly present IB or A-Level qualifications, both of which natively produce predicted grades).
predicted_grades.by_whom: Where used (non-EU/direct route only): issued by the applicant's own school/teachers under the rules of their home qualification (IB, A-Level), not generated or estimated by any Irish body. Within the CAO/points route, there is no predicted-grade artifact of any kind, native or foreign, that CAO itself acts upon.
predicted_grades.for_what: Where used, to allow a non-EU applicant's file to be assessed and an offer considered ahead of final results being known — functionally the same purpose predicted grades serve in the UK, but confined (on the evidence found this pass) to the non-EU/direct pipeline rather than being a system-wide Irish mechanism.
predicted_grades.conditional_offer_relationship: Not established within the CAO/points route in the predicted-grade sense (there is no forward-looking target grade to be conditional upon; see conditional_vs_unconditional_admission section for the different, narrower senses of 'conditional' that do exist there). Plausibly linked within the non-EU/direct route — a Trinity-style application built on predicted scores would logically require some later confirmation step once final results are issued — but this research pass did not locate an explicit Irish HEI offer-letter example using UCAS-style 'conditional offer' terminology; this should be treated as a reasonable inference from the accepted-documentation list, not a directly sourced confirmation.
predicted_grades.final_result_requirement: Yes, universally — even within the non-EU/direct route where predicted scores are accepted at application stage, actual final results are ultimately required before enrolment. Within the CAO/points route, final results are required before any offer is even issued, not merely before enrolment is finalised.

conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.concept_exists: Yes, but in a materially narrower and differently-structured sense within the CAO/points route than in the UK or Netherlands, plus a separate, more UK-like sense that appears to exist only within the non-EU/direct route.
conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.explanation: Within the CAO/points route: there is no predicted-grade-conditional offer at all (no offer issues until actual results are known — see predicted_grades). What resembles 'conditionality' here is purely sequencing/logistics, not a forward-looking academic target: restricted-course early assessment (portfolio, interview, HPAT) can occur months before Leaving Certificate results, but the resulting points-based offer still only issues once actual results are known and combined with that earlier assessment score — the early step does not itself constitute an offer. Round A/Round Zero (mature, deferred, graduate-entry medicine, QQI/FET, some non-EU/visa-timing applicants) can receive offers before the main Leaving Certificate results date specifically because these applicant categories typically already hold final, already-known results from an earlier period — not because a prediction is being acted upon. Within the non-EU/direct route: Trinity's acceptance of 'Predicted Scores' as application-stage evidence implies a genuine, UK-like conditional-offer mechanism (offer contingent on achieving a stated final result) is operating, though this research pass did not verify an actual offer-letter example using that terminology.

subject_prerequisites.pattern: Real and programme-specific, but structurally different from the Netherlands' VWO 'profielen' model: the Leaving Certificate has no fixed, small set of named national subject-combination tracks — students choose roughly 7-8 subjects individually (subject to school-timetabling practicalities), and programmes then publish their own specific subject/grade prerequisites on top of that open structure, most commonly a named minimum Higher Level Mathematics grade, and for some fields a lab science. Higher Level Mathematics carries a national +25 CAO-points bonus (for grade H6 or above) that functions as a strong incentive layer distinct from, and additional to, any hard subject requirement a specific course sets.
subject_prerequisites.scope: programme (individual course codes set their own subject/grade prerequisites; the national Leaving Certificate structure itself imposes no fixed subject-combination requirement analogous to VWO profielen)
illustrative_examples: UCD's non-EU entry table shows explicit, programme-differentiated Mathematics minimums: 'C2 3rd level / 4.5 Lise' for Business/Computer Science/Engineering-track programmes, 'B3 3rd level' for the Engineering Omnibus, 'D1 3rd level / 2 Lise' for Economics/Social Science/Agricultural Science programmes — i.e., the required Mathematics standard is set per programme, not uniformly.

CAO's own EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines note generally that 'for some HEIs Mathematics is required for matriculation' in addition to the general floor, and that 'there are specific subject requirements for most courses' beyond matriculation.
Medicine and Veterinary Medicine require specific lab-science subjects (e.g., UCD's non-EU Veterinary Medicine entry specifies a Chemistry requirement) alongside the general Mathematics standard.
Higher Level Mathematics' +25-point CAO bonus is applied nationally regardless of programme, but only actually lifts an applicant's total if Higher Level Mathematics is among their best 6 subjects.
subject_prerequisites.vwo_profielen_detail: Not applicable — Ireland has no equivalent fixed-track subject-combination structure. This is a genuine structural difference from the Netherlands worth naming explicitly: the Leaving Certificate is closer to an à-la-carte subject list (with matriculation-level and course-level constraints layered on afterward) than to a small number of named national profiles.

standardized_tests.mandatory_optional_status: No SAT/ACT-style general admissions test exists within the domestic CAO/points route. HPAT-Ireland (Health Professions Admission Test) is mandatory nationally for admission to EVERY undergraduate Medicine programme at all 6 Irish medical schools (University of Galway, University of Limerick, Trinity College Dublin, UCC, UCD, and RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences) — an aptitude test (logical reasoning, interpersonal understanding, non-verbal reasoning), not a subject-knowledge test, sat in the applicant's year of entry (typically around February/March, before Leaving Certificate results). SAT/ACT appear only within the non-EU/international direct-application pipeline (e.g., as an alternative route within UCD's and UCC's Turkey-specific tables, and as part of Trinity's 'US High School Diploma with SAT or ACT' accepted direct-entry qualification) — confirming these are not a domestic/CAO-route phenomenon at all.
standardized_tests.current_cycle_note: The HPAT/Leaving-Certificate combination is undergoing a confirmed structural change between the current cycle and 2027 entry. Currently (through 2026 entry): a minimum of 480 Leaving Certificate points is required, Leaving Certificate points above 550 are moderated (scaled) up to a maximum of 565, and HPAT is scored to a maximum of 300 — combining to a maximum possible total of 865. From 2027 entry: Leaving Certificate points above 550 will no longer be moderated (full points apply, to the ordinary 625 maximum), while HPAT's maximum weighting drops from 300 to 150 — combining to a new maximum of 775, and the 480-point minimum plus the requirement to sit HPAT in the year of entry both remain unchanged. This represents a substantial rebalancing toward Leaving Certificate results and away from HPAT for the 2027 cycle specifically — flag any cited HPAT/points weighting as cycle-specific.
programme_specific_tests: HPAT-Ireland: mandatory for all undergraduate Medicine applicants nationally, at all 6 medical schools, combined with Leaving Certificate points as described above.

Restricted/portfolio courses (e.g., National College of Art & Design) run their own early-assessment procedures (portfolio submission, sometimes as early as February) as part of CAO's 'restricted-application' course category — see restricted_selective_programmes section.

language_requirements.framework: For CAO/EU-EFTA-UK-route applicants, English-language proficiency is normally satisfied automatically through the qualification itself: a Leaving Certificate result of at least H7/O6 in English, or a GCE A-level applicant's GCSE English Language grade 4/C or better. Where the qualification does not include a sufficient English result, or the result is more than 2 years old, an approved English test is required: IELTS Academic (average 6.5 across all components, minimum 6.0 in each band; the CAO Guidelines note a 2026-only acceptance of the 'IELTS indicator' variant, under review), Duolingo English Test (score 120, minimum 110 in each subscore), English Test for Academic and Professional Purposes (ETAPP, grade C1 or better), IELCA Academic (minimum 35, minimum 33 per band), or LanguageCert B2 Communicator (High Pass, no less than 33 per skill). These are explicitly stated minimums — 'there may be higher levels required for matriculation and/or particular programmes in individual institutions.'
language_requirements.exemption_pattern: Built into the framework rather than a separate carve-out: applicants whose qualifying exam (Leaving Certificate, A-level, or an EU country's own matriculation exam with English presented as a subject at an acceptable level) already demonstrates sufficient English do not need a separate test, unless that result is more than 2 years old.
language_requirements.where_variation_begins: At the HEI/programme level for the exact minimum score, and structurally at the route level: the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK figures above are a JOINTLY AGREED baseline across participating HEIs (not CAO's own unilateral rule), while the non-EU/direct route is more fragmented — each HEI's international office sets and publishes its own English-proficiency policy independently (e.g., Trinity requires 'a recognised certificate of English Language Competency' per its own accepted-test list; UCD's Foundation Programme cites IELTS in roughly the 4.5-5.5 range as an entry-to-foundation bar, distinct from any direct-degree-entry threshold). Ireland's status as an English-speaking country does not remove this requirement for non-native-English applicants, including Turkish applicants specifically, who must supply English-proficiency evidence through one of these routes.

application_timing.cycle: 2026-2027 academic year (entry September/October 2026), cited alongside CAO mechanics that structurally repeat each year (2027-2028 entry expected to follow the same November-opening / 1 February normal-deadline / 1 May late-deadline / 1 July change-of-mind pattern, though exact 2027 dates should be re-verified closer to that cycle).
application_timing.major_deadline_pattern: The CAO application portal for 2026-2027 entry opened 5 November 2025. An early/discounted online-application rate applied to a mid-to-late-January closing point (commonly cited as 20 January, at a lower fee than the normal rate — figure secondary-corroborated, not independently primary-verified this pass). The NORMAL closing date was 1 February 2026 at 17:00. LATE applications remained possible from 5 March 2026 (secondary-sourced reopening date) up to a final LATE closing date of 1 May 2026 at 17:00, at a higher fee; late applicants forfeit consideration for the HEAR/DARE access schemes and for mature-applicant assessment.
application_timing.change_of_mind_facility: A free 'Change of Mind' facility lets applicants add, remove, or reorder their ranked course list without needing to have applied to each HEI separately, at these 2026-cycle windows (Citizens Information, sourced to CAO): free from 5 November 2025 to 1 February 2026 (17:00); a EUR 10 fee applied from 5 February to 1 March 2026; free again from 5 May to the final Change of Mind deadline of 1 July 2026 (17:00). This lets an applicant revise their genuine order of preference even after sitting their Leaving Certificate exams (typically completed by mid-June) but before their results (and thus their actual points total) are known — a structurally important strategic window with no direct UK/UCAS equivalent.
application_timing.results_and_offers: Leaving Certificate results for the 2026 cycle were published 21 August 2026 (cycle-specific date; results are always released mid-to-late August, via the State Examinations Commission's Candidate Self Service Portal). CAO offer rounds for the 2026 cycle: Round A (non-standard applicants not awaiting current-year results, e.g., mature/deferred/some non-EU visa-timing cases) — offers 6 July 2026, reply by 9 July; Round Zero (graduate-entry medicine and other early categories) — offers 6 August; Round One (the main body of offers, issued shortly after Leaving Certificate results) — offers 26 August, reply by 1 September; Rounds Two through Five continued through September as declined/unfilled places cascade to the next-highest-ranked eligible applicant on each list, with the final round issuing 29 September.
application_timing.restricted_course_timing: Restricted-application courses (portfolio/interview/aptitude-assessed) can require their own separate early-assessment step well before the main results/offer timeline — e.g., a National College of Art & Design portfolio submission as early as February of the application year — layered on top of, not instead of, the main CAO points timeline.

constraints: Up to 10 Level 8 course preferences and up to 10 Level 6/7 course preferences may be ranked simultaneously via CAO (two separate lists) — sourced to Citizens Information's official walkthrough; the precise 'up to 10 per list' reading (rather than 10 total across both lists) is inferred from the application form's two separate 'Add Level 8' / 'Add Level 7/6' entry points described in the same source and is consistent with long-standing CAO practice, but was not confirmed against a directly quoted CAO Handbook sentence this pass.

No numerus-fixus-style national cap on how many 'restricted' or high-points courses an applicant may list was found — structurally, this kind of cap appears unnecessary in Ireland's system because essentially all Level 8 courses (not a separate capped subset) already run through the same points-competitive mechanism.

Restricted-application courses require early action: the course must be added to the CAO application in time for the HEI to arrange its own early assessment (sometimes as early as February), independent of the main 1 February/1 May deadlines.

HEAR/DARE (equity-access schemes for socioeconomically disadvantaged or disabled applicants) have their own, earlier internal deadlines (2026 cycle: form completion by 1 March, supporting documents by 10 March) distinct from the general course-preference deadlines, and are unavailable to late applicants entirely.

The Change of Mind facility (free to 1 February, a small fee in a mid-window, free again 5 May-1 July) allows genuine order-of-preference revision after sitting exams but before results are known — a distinctive strategic lever with no direct UK/UCAS equivalent.

Non-EU/direct applicants face a fundamentally separate strategic calculus: no shared ranked-preference list, no Change-of-Mind-style mechanism, and per-HEI (sometimes per-course) application fees, each with its own deadline (e.g., Trinity's non-EU applications commonly cite a priority deadline around 1 February with general applications remaining open considerably later, subject to availability).
application_strategy_constraints.explanation: Ireland's strategy constraints are structured around a single shared ranked list executed by one national point-ranking engine (for the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route), which is a materially different strategic environment from the Netherlands' per-programme-capped registration model or the UK's 5-choice/firm-insurance model — see admissions_decision_model for the full contrast.

personal_statement_essays.role: Not a feature of the CAO/points route at all for standard courses — the complete official application walkthrough (account creation, qualification details, course preferences, HEAR/DARE flags, Statement of Application Record) contains no essay, personal statement, or statement-of-purpose step anywhere. It IS a required, individually-reviewed document within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route: Trinity's general international undergraduate admissions requirements explicitly list 'A 500-word statement of purpose' among required application documents (and the same requirement applies to its Foundation Programme applications).
personal_statement_essays.explanation: This is a route-level distinction, not a universal Irish feature or a universal absence: essays are essentially structurally absent from the shared CAO points mechanism (there is no field for one to occupy in a purely points-ranked process) but present as a genuine, individually-assessed requirement once an applicant is in the separate, HEI-run non-EU pipeline.

recommendation_letters.role: Same route-level pattern as personal statements. Absent entirely from the CAO/points route for standard courses. Required within the non-EU/direct-to-university route: Trinity's general international undergraduate requirements list 'Two academic references' among required documents (also required for its Foundation Programme).
recommendation_letters.explanation: Confirms a genuine structural split rather than a uniform Irish policy: the domestic points-ranked mechanism has no channel for a recommendation letter to influence a decision, while the separate non-EU pipeline treats references as a standard, expected document — much closer to the US/UK pattern than to the CAO pattern.

extracurricular_activities.role: Essentially no role at all within the CAO/points route for standard courses — a stronger, more absolute 'not a factor' finding than in any other country in this research package so far. The CAO points score is computed purely and mechanically from the best 6 Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) subject grades plus the Higher Level Mathematics bonus; there is no motivation-letter-style channel (as exists for the Netherlands' numerus fixus programmes) through which activity evidence could enter the standard points calculation at all.
extracurricular_activities.nuance: The one genuine non-exam-grade lever within the domestic system is the HEAR/DARE scheme, which awards reduced-points access-route places to applicants who document socioeconomic disadvantage (HEAR) or disability-related educational disadvantage (DARE) — a context/equity mechanism, not an achievement- or activity-breadth credit, and available only to eligible applicants who apply for it by its own earlier deadline. Within the separate non-EU/direct route, some HEIs request a CV alongside the transcript/references/SOP for non-EU applications, implying some soft consideration of activities/experience exists there, though far less structured than US-style holistic review. One narrow, programme-specific exception exists: UCD's non-EU Veterinary Medicine entry requires documented, dated practical animal-handling experience (a minimum of 60 hours across at least 2 of 4 named animal categories, within the 3 years before entry) as a hard entry requirement — a genuine activity/experience requirement, but scoped to this one restricted programme, not general.

interviews_tests_portfolios.pattern: Concentrated in named restricted/professional categories rather than spread broadly. HPAT-Ireland (aptitude test) is mandatory for all domestic/CAO-route undergraduate Medicine applicants at all 6 medical schools. Portfolio submission (and CAO's own 'Restricted' flag on the course-choice form) applies to Art & Design-type courses (e.g., National College of Art & Design), with assessment sometimes beginning as early as February. Within the non-EU/direct route, at least one HEI (UCD) layers an interview requirement onto its non-EU Medicine entry criteria specifically ('89% Lise & 3.2/4.0 in degree or 99% Lise & 1340 SAT + Interview'), distinct from — and apparently not routed through — the domestic HPAT mechanism, since UCD's non-EU Medicine table makes no mention of HPAT or Leaving Certificate points at all.
interviews_tests_portfolios.when_applicable: Only for specific restricted/professional/practice-based programmes (Medicine via HPAT domestically, or via a separate interview-based non-EU route at some HEIs; Art/Design via portfolio); not applicable to standard points-based Level 8/7/6 courses, where meeting matriculation plus achieving the emergent points cutoff is sufficient.

restricted_selective_programmes.numerus_fixus_explanation: Ireland uses CAO's own term 'restricted-application course' for programmes requiring early assessment (portfolio, interview, aptitude test) beyond the standard points mechanism, and treats Medicine as its own separate, heavily documented case via HPAT. This is a narrower and more consistently-named category than the Netherlands' numerus fixus/capaciteitsfixus: Ireland does not appear to have (on the evidence found this pass) a broad, legally-defined, shifting national list of capacity-capped fields covering Psychology, several Engineering/CS programmes, and more, the way the Netherlands' 2023 legal framework does. Capacity limits plausibly apply to other health-professional programmes (Nursing, Dentistry, Physiotherapy) given their reliance on clinical placement capacity, but specific quota figures or a formal 'restricted' designation for these beyond Medicine were not independently sourced this pass — a genuine gap, not a confirmed absence.
restricted_selective_programmes.current_mechanism: For Medicine specifically: a dual points-plus-aptitude-test mechanism, not a lottery or qualitative-panel-review system. A minimum of 480 Leaving Certificate points is required; points above 550 are currently moderated up to a 565 maximum; HPAT-Ireland is scored to a current maximum of 300; the two combine to a current maximum of 865. This is changing for 2027 entry: moderation above 550 is being removed (full points to the 625 maximum apply) while HPAT's maximum weighting is reduced to 150, producing a new combined maximum of 775 — a rebalancing that increases the relative influence of Leaving Certificate performance and reduces HPAT's relative weight, while leaving the 480-point floor and the requirement to sit HPAT in the year of entry unchanged. For Art & Design/portfolio-based restricted courses: an early qualitative portfolio (and sometimes interview) assessment run by the HEI, combined with (not replacing) the points mechanism. Non-EU/direct-route restricted courses (e.g., UCD's non-EU Medicine) can run an entirely separate mechanism (interview-based, points-and-HPAT-free) from the domestic CAO/HPAT pathway for the same named degree.
example_fields: Medicine (Geneeskunde-equivalent; all 6 Irish medical schools) — HPAT + Leaving Certificate points, 480-point floor
Veterinary Medicine — points-based domestically, with UCD's non-EU route additionally requiring documented practical animal-handling experience
Art & Design (e.g., National College of Art & Design) — portfolio-based, CAO-flagged '(Restricted)'

Other CAO-flagged 'Restricted' courses with early interview/assessment procedures — the specific full national list was not independently rendered from CAO's own Restrictions page in this research pass

admissions_decision_model.dominant_model: A genuinely distinct third architecture from every country covered so far in this research package — neither the Netherlands' bifurcated threshold-vs-selection model, nor the UK's single-shared-platform-but-individually-reviewed model, nor the US's per-institution holistic review.
admissions_decision_model.explanation: For the large majority of Level 8/7/6 courses accessed via CAO: admission is COMPETITIVE-BY-POINTS, essentially universally, not just for a capped 'restricted' subset. Meeting matriculation (the eligibility floor) is necessary but not sufficient — CAO's own jointly-authored guidance states this explicitly ('attainment of the minimum eligibility criteria does not guarantee a place. A points scoring system is in operation'). Each course code has an emergent, cycle-specific points cutoff determined only once that year's actual applicant pool and results are known, set by the balance between the HEI-specified place count and applicant demand — 'it is not possible to forecast how many points will be required for a particular course until the current year's examination results are known.' Critically, this competitive ranking is executed by CAO's OWN shared computational system on the HEI's instructions, not reviewed applicant-by-applicant by university admissions staff for standard courses — a genuinely different division of labour from the UK (where UCAS routes applications but university staff individually review and decide) and from the Netherlands (where Studielink performs no ranking function at all). Restricted/professional programmes (Medicine via HPAT, Art/Design via portfolio) layer a second, qualitative or aptitude dimension onto this same points-based core rather than replacing it. The non-EU/direct-to-university route operates as a genuinely separate model again: individualised, HEI-reviewed, evidence-based (transcript, references, SOP, sometimes predicted grades and interview), inside an explicitly capacity-limited quota at some HEIs (UCD states non-EU applicants compete for 'a limited number of places' in most courses) — closer in kind to the US/UK model than to the domestic CAO mechanism.

safe_inferences: It is safe to infer that, within the CAO/points route, no offer for a standard course will be made before the applicant's actual final results (Leaving Certificate, IB, A-Level, etc.) are known — Ireland's is a strict post-qualification-admissions system, and predicted grades play no role in this route regardless of the applicant's home curriculum.

It is safe to infer that meeting matriculation eligibility does NOT equal admission for CAO/points-route Level 8 courses in general — unlike the Netherlands' open (non-numerus-fixus) programmes, competitiveness-by-points is the norm across virtually all Level 8 courses in Ireland, not an exception confined to a capped subset.

It is safe to infer that a specific numeric points figure or cutoff for any given course in a given year is NOT a stable target — cutoffs are cycle-specific and emerge only from that year's actual results and applicant demand.

It is safe to infer that essays, personal statements, and recommendation letters play no role in the standard CAO/points route, but that they DO appear as genuine, individually-assessed requirements within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university application route.

It is safe to infer that a Turkish (or other non-EU) applicant's acceptance of a given qualification (notably a plain Lise Diplomasi) by one Irish university does not imply acceptance by another — UCD, UCC, and Trinity apply materially different, independently-set policies to the identical qualification.

It is safe to infer that HPAT is required for every domestic-route undergraduate Medicine applicant nationally, with no university-level exception, though the exact HPAT/points weighting is cycle-specific (materially different from 2027 entry onward).
unsafe_inferences: It is unsafe to assume Ireland's admissions timing/mechanics mirror the UK's simply because both are English-speaking and geographically close — the CAO/points route's post-qualification, actual-results-only model is a sharp structural departure from UCAS's predicted-grade-driven conditional-offer system.

It is unsafe to assume CAO is a pure registration/routing platform like Studielink or (for the vast majority of its function) UCAS — for standard courses, CAO's own system computationally executes the points-ranking/allocation decision on the HEIs' instructions, a materially more active role than either of those platforms play.

It is unsafe to assume all non-EU/international applicants go through CAO — the default for non-EU-fee-status applicants is direct application to each HEI, though a specific HEI may still instruct particular non-EU applicant categories to use CAO (e.g., for visa-timing reasons via Round A/Round Zero).

It is unsafe to assume a Turkish applicant's plain Lise Diplomasi is either uniformly accepted or uniformly rejected for direct entry across Irish universities — UCD and UCC publish direct-entry percentage tables accepting it; Trinity does not accept it for direct entry at all.

It is unsafe to assume Turkey's national university entrance exam (YKS, or its pre-2018 predecessor LYS) is either required or irrelevant to Dutch-style — sorry, Irish-university Turkish-applicant assessment at a system level — UCC's page implies a requirement (under outdated terminology) while UCD's does not mention it; this is a genuine, unresolved, university-specific split.

It is unsafe to assume extracurricular activities are irrelevant everywhere in the Irish system just because they play no role in the CAO/points route — the non-EU/direct route appears to weigh CV/experience content to some degree, and specific restricted programmes (e.g., UCD's non-EU Veterinary Medicine) impose their own concrete experience requirements.

It is unsafe to assume the current HPAT/Leaving-Certificate points-weighting figures (480 minimum, 865 combined maximum) remain valid past the 2026 entry cycle — a confirmed, named change takes effect for 2027 entry (775 new combined maximum, no moderation above 550, HPAT capped at 150).

eligibility_competitiveness_fit.eligibility: Within the CAO/points route: an objective, checkable matriculation floor (subject count and grade thresholds, e.g., 6 subjects at O6+ including 2-3 at H5+ for Level 8) plus any programme-specific subject prerequisites — binary, not graded, and NOT itself the basis for the actual admission decision.
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.competitiveness: The dominant, near-universal factor for CAO/points-route Level 8/7/6 admission — a sharp contrast with the Netherlands, where competitiveness is confined to numerus fixus programmes specifically. In Ireland, essentially every points-based course has an emergent, cycle-specific points cutoff that determines actual admission, making 'eligible' and 'admitted' distinct outcomes for the great majority of popular courses, not just a capped minority. However, this competitiveness is measured through a SINGLE variable (total points, from 6 best subject grades plus any Mathematics bonus) for standard courses — a meaningfully narrower, more mechanical form of 'competitive' than the US's multi-factor holistic review or the Netherlands' numerus fixus qualitative/lottery/hybrid selection. Restricted/professional programmes (Medicine, Art/Design) add one further qualitative or aptitude dimension (HPAT, portfolio) on top of this single-variable core.
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.fit: Essentially absent as an independently assessed concept within the CAO/points route for standard courses — there is no essay, interview, or holistic-review mechanism through which a university could evaluate 'fit' for most programmes; whatever fit-like signal exists is folded into the points-plus-subject-prerequisite mechanism itself (does the applicant's coursework and points level match this specific course's demonstrated demand/requirements) rather than being a separate qualitative judgment. Fit becomes a more explicit, separately-assessed concept only within restricted/portfolio courses and within the non-EU/direct-to-university route, where references, SOP, and (at some HEIs) interviews create genuine channels for a qualitative fit judgment.

counselor_actions: Explain the two-layer eligibility/competitiveness structure clearly to students and families: meeting matriculation is only a floor, not a guarantee, and the actual points cutoff for any specific course is unknowable in advance of that year's results — avoid promising a specific points target as a safe outcome.

For students also targeting UK universities via UCAS, explicitly flag the timing mismatch: UCAS relies on predicted grades for conditional offers made well before final results, while CAO makes no offer at all for standard courses until actual Leaving Certificate/IB/A-Level results are published in August — plan application strategy and expectation-setting around both timelines separately.

For a Turkish (or other non-EU) applicant, do not generalise one Irish university's Lise Diploması policy to another — proactively check each specific target university's own published non-EU/international entry table (UCD and UCC publish detailed percentage-based tables; Trinity requires IB/A-Level/AP+SAT or its Foundation Programme instead) and verify directly with the university whether YKS/national-exam results are required, since this is unresolved and inconsistently documented across sources.

For students targeting Medicine, confirm HPAT registration timing (typically registration opens in the year of entry, ahead of Leaving Certificate results) and communicate that the domestic HPAT/points combination is changing for 2027 entry (reduced HPAT weighting, full unmoderated Leaving Certificate points) — do not rely on this cycle's exact weighting for a 2027-entry student.

Encourage students to use the free Change of Mind window (through 1 February, and again 5 May-1 July) to keep their CAO list in genuine order of preference, especially after sitting (but before receiving results for) their Leaving Certificate/IB/A-Level exams — remind students the list should reflect genuine preference, not a strategic guess at their own performance, since CAO cannot move an applicant down their own list.

Flag restricted-application courses (Art & Design, and any course marked 'Restricted' on the CAO system) early — some require portfolio or assessment steps as early as February of the application year, well before the general deadlines.

For non-EU applicants generally, set expectations that they are very likely applying OUTSIDE the CAO points system, directly to each HEI's own international office, with its own transcript/reference/SOP/English-proficiency package, its own fee, its own deadline, and — for HEIs like UCD — competing within an explicitly capped non-EU quota rather than against a simple points cutoff.

Where a target university does not accept a student's qualification for direct entry (e.g., Trinity and a plain Lise Diploması), plan an International Foundation Programme route well in advance — these are typically one year long with their own separate (often lower) English-proficiency entry bar and, at some institutions, guaranteed progression to the named degree on successful completion.

data_model_implications.notes: Ireland requires ORYN's data model to represent admission facts across at least five distinct dimensions, one more than the Netherlands' four-layer model: (1) route (CAO/EU-EFTA-UK vs. non-EU/direct-to-HEI — these are not just different platforms but different EVIDENCE models: actual-results-only vs. predicted-grades-accepted; no-essay vs. essay-required; shared-ranked-list vs. per-HEI-independent), (2) national/platform (CAO's shared points-ranking mechanics and the H1-H8/O1-O8 scale, uniform for all CAO-route applicants regardless of HEI), (3) recognition-baseline (QQI/NARIC's advisory-only comparability statements, and separately CAO's jointly-HEI-authored EU/EFTA/UK matriculation/IPS tables — both non-binding on any individual admission decision), (4) university (non-EU/Turkey-specific entry tables that differ sharply between UCD, UCC, and Trinity for the identical input qualification), and (5) course-code/cycle (the actual points cutoff for a specific course in a specific year, which is emergent and unknowable in advance, and the specific HPAT/points weighting formula, which is itself scheduled to change between the current and 2027 entry cycles). A model that stores one 'Ireland requirement' record per qualification type, or even one per university, would still miss the course-code-and-cycle-level variation that determines actual admission for the large majority of Irish courses.
gaps: Whether Turkey's national entrance exam (YKS, or its pre-2018 predecessor LYS, as apparently still named on at least one university page) is genuinely required for Turkish-applicant direct entry is unresolved and inconsistent across the three universities sourced.

Exact current CAO application fee figures were not independently confirmed against a primary cao.ie fee page in this research pass (direct fetch attempts returned errors); the commonly cited figures (an early/discounted rate, a normal rate around EUR 50, a higher late rate around EUR 60-65) should be treated as secondary-corroborated, not primary-verified.

Whether the CAO course-choice limit is precisely '10 Level 8 + 10 Level 6/7' (20 total) or some other precise figure was inferred from Citizens Information's description of the application form's structure rather than a directly quoted CAO Handbook sentence.

Whether non-Medicine health-professional programmes (Nursing, Dentistry, Physiotherapy) carry HSE-linked national quota figures or a formal 'restricted' designation comparable to Medicine's was not independently sourced this pass.

The full national list of CAO-flagged 'Restricted' courses beyond the illustrative examples found (Medicine via HPAT, Art & Design via portfolio) was not independently rendered from CAO's own Restrictions page in this research pass.

Whether an actual Irish HEI offer letter uses UCAS-style 'conditional offer' terminology for non-EU applicants presenting predicted grades was not directly observed; this remains an inference from Trinity's accepted-documentation list rather than a confirmed finding.

system_university_programme_override_mod.explanation: Layer 1 (route): whether an applicant uses the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK mechanism or applies direct to an HEI is determined by fee status (EU/EFTA/UK vs. non-EU), and this single fact changes almost every subsequent layer of evidence, timing, and decision-making described in this document — it is the most consequential single branching point in the Irish system and should be treated as a first-class routing decision in ORYN's model, not a minor metadata flag. Layer 2 (national/platform, CAO route only): the H1-H8/O1-O8 points scale, the Higher Level Mathematics bonus, matriculation floors, and the shared Round A/Zero/One-Five offer-round mechanics are uniform across all CAO-route applicants and HEIs — no individual university can waive or alter these. Layer 3 (national credential-recognition baseline): QQI/NARIC's advisory comparability statements, and, for the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route specifically, the jointly-HEI-authored (not CAO-authored) Guidelines document's country-by-country matriculation and IPS tables — both establish a starting reference point that individual decisions draw on but are not themselves binding admission decisions. Layer 4 (university): each HEI sets its own subject prerequisites, its own place count per course code (which drives that course's emergent points cutoff), and — critically, for non-EU/direct applicants — its own entirely independent entry-requirement policy, most sharply illustrated by the Turkish Lise Diploması split between UCD/UCC (direct entry via a published percentage table) and Trinity (not accepted for direct entry at all). Layer 5 (course code and cycle): the actual points cutoff for a specific course in a specific year is not set in advance by any layer above — it emerges from that cycle's specific balance of HEI-specified place count against applicant demand, and for Medicine specifically, the HPAT/points combination formula itself is scheduled to change between the current and 2027 entry cycles. ORYN should never present a Layer 4 or Layer 5 fact (a specific university's Turkey table, or a specific course's points requirement in a specific past year) as if it were a Layer 1-3 national fact, and should never treat a past year's points requirement as a reliable predictor of a future cycle's cutoff.

matrix_row.main_application_architecture: Centralized platform (CAO) that both processes applications AND computationally executes points-based ranking/allocation on behalf of HEIs for standard courses; HEIs formally retain the admissions decision and set course-level criteria/place counts, but CAO's own system performs the ranking execution — a third model distinct from UCAS's human-reviewed routing and Studielink's registration-only role. Non-EU/international applicants generally bypass CAO entirely and apply direct to each HEI.
matrix_row.central_platform: CAO (Central Applications Office) — required for EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants (and any HEI-instructed non-EU categories); a private company jointly run by participating HEIs, not a government body
matrix_row.direct_applications_possible: Yes, and it is the DEFAULT route for non-EU/international-fee-status applicants (straight to each HEI's own international office); EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants must generally use CAO instead of direct application for CAO-listed courses
matrix_row.application_choice_limits: Up to 10 Level 8 preferences plus up to 10 Level 6/7 preferences via CAO (two separate ranked lists); no numerus-fixus-style cap on 'selective' choices, since virtually all Level 8 courses already run through the same unified points mechanism
matrix_row.predicted_grades_role: Not used at all within the CAO/points route for any applicant category or curriculum — a strict post-qualification-admissions system that waits for actual final results (confirmed even for IB, whose native predicted grades are bypassed in favour of CAO accessing actual final results directly). Predicted grades DO appear to be used within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route (e.g., Trinity accepts 'Predicted Scores' for undergraduate non-EU applications) — a genuine two-track split not seen elsewhere in this research package
matrix_row.subject_prerequisites: Real and programme-specific (commonly a named Higher Level Mathematics standard, sometimes a lab science), layered onto an à-la-carte Leaving Certificate with no Dutch-style fixed 'profiel' subject-combination structure; Higher Level Mathematics carries a national +25-point bonus that functions as an incentive rather than a universal hard requirement
matrix_row.standardized_tests: No SAT/ACT role in the domestic CAO/points route; HPAT-Ireland is mandatory nationally for all undergraduate Medicine applicants at all 6 medical schools, combined with Leaving Certificate points to a moderated total (weighting formula changing for 2027 entry); SAT/ACT appear only within the non-EU/international direct-application pipeline
matrix_row.language_proof: CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route: Leaving Cert English H7/O6 or A-level GCSE English grade 4/C generally sufficient, otherwise IELTS Academic 6.5 average/6.0 per band (or Duolingo/ETAPP/IELCA/LanguageCert equivalents) as a jointly HEI-agreed minimum baseline that individual HEIs/courses may set higher. Non-EU/direct route: each HEI sets its own policy independently, more fragmented
matrix_row.essays_motivation: Not a feature of the CAO/points route at all for standard courses (no essay/SOP step anywhere in the process); required within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route (e.g., Trinity requires a 500-word statement of purpose for non-EU undergraduate applications)
matrix_row.recommendations: Same pattern as essays — structurally absent from the CAO/points route; required within the non-EU/direct pipeline (e.g., Trinity requires two academic references for non-EU undergraduate applications)
matrix_row.extracurricular_role: Essentially no role in the CAO/points route for standard courses — points are computed purely from best-6 Leaving Certificate subject grades plus any Mathematics bonus; the one genuine non-exam lever domestically is the HEAR/DARE equity-access scheme (reduced-points route for documented socioeconomic disadvantage/disability), which addresses context, not achievement breadth
matrix_row.conditional_offers: Not in the UK predicted-grade sense within the CAO/points route (no offer issues until actual final results are known for any applicant category); a genuine conditional-offer-like mechanism (accepting predicted scores at application stage) appears to operate within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route, though not verified via an actual offer-letter example this pass
matrix_row.restricted_programmes: A narrower, more consistently-named set than the Netherlands' numerus fixus: Medicine (HPAT + points, uniform across all 6 medical schools), Art & Design/Architecture-type courses (portfolio, CAO-flagged '(Restricted)'), and other early-assessment courses; no broad, shifting, legally-defined national capacity-cap category comparable to the Netherlands' capaciteitsfixus was found in this research pass
matrix_row.turkiye_meb_direct_entry_complexity: High and genuinely university-specific, more sharply split than in any other country researched so far: Turkish applicants fall entirely outside the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK points system and apply direct to each HEI, which sets its own independent criteria — UCD and UCC both publish direct-entry Lise Diploması percentage tables (roughly 67-100% depending on programme), while Trinity does not accept the plain Lise Diploması for direct entry at all (requiring IB/A-Level/AP+SAT, or its International Foundation Programme otherwise)
matrix_row.dominant_counselor_risk: Assuming Ireland's admissions system works like the UK's next door — either assuming UCAS-style predicted-grade-driven conditional offers exist within the domestic CAO route (they do not; CAO is strictly post-qualification/actual-results-based) or assuming CAO is a pure registration/routing layer like Studielink/UCAS rather than the shared computational ranking engine it actually operates for points courses; specific to Turkish applicants, assuming one Irish university's Lise Diploması percentage table or foundation-year requirement generalises to another, when UCD/UCC's direct-entry tables and Trinity's foundation-year-only stance are genuinely, sharply different, independently-set policies.

unresolved_questions: Whether Turkey's national university entrance exam (YKS, or the pre-2018 'LYS' name still used on at least one Irish university page) is genuinely required for Turkish-applicant direct entry — UCC's page implies a requirement under apparently outdated terminology; UCD's detailed programme-by-programme Turkey table does not mention it at all.

Exact, primary-verified current CAO application fee figures (early/normal/late) — direct attempts to fetch CAO's own fee page did not succeed this pass; cited figures rest on secondary aggregator sources.

The precise CAO course-choice limit wording (10 Level 8 + 10 Level 6/7 as two separate lists, versus some other precise structure) — inferred from Citizens Information's description of the application form rather than a directly quoted CAO Handbook sentence.

Whether non-Medicine health-professional undergraduate programmes (Nursing, Dentistry, Physiotherapy, etc.) carry HSE-linked national quota figures or CAO's formal 'Restricted' designation, and if so, on what mechanism (pure points vs. points-plus-test) — not independently sourced this pass.

The complete, current, national list of CAO-flagged 'Restricted' courses beyond the illustrative examples confirmed here (Medicine, Art & Design) — CAO's own Restrictions page content did not fully render in this research pass.

Whether an actual Irish HEI offer letter to a non-EU applicant uses explicit UCAS-style 'conditional offer' terminology when predicted grades are presented — inferred from Trinity's accepted-documentation list (which names 'Predicted Scores' as acceptable), not directly observed in an offer example.

Whether financial proof of means plays any role in the admission DECISION itself (as distinct from post-offer visa/immigration requirements) at any Irish HEI — no source reviewed this pass identified it as an admissions-decision factor; treated as a confirmed non-factor for the admissions architecture specifically, separate from immigration mechanics which are out of scope for this research.
